summary: Evaluates existing GMPLS protocols and mechanisms against the requirements for Multi-Layer Networks and Multi-Region Networks. It points out where more protocol extensions or procedures are needed and gives guidelines for them. It is informational and does not itself define new protocol.

eli5.summary: This is a report card on existing network tools: can they handle networks with several layers and regions? It lists where they fall short and what might be added.

questions: what is a hybrid node in networking
subtitle: Assessing GMPLS protocols for layered multi-region networks.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to manage multiple switching layers and regions under unified control, but existing GMPLS protocols may not fully support multi-layer and multi-region requirements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5339 evaluates which existing GMPLS mechanisms address these requirements and identifies gaps where new protocol extensions or procedures are needed.
tldr.outcome: The evaluation identifies six areas requiring protocol extensions: virtual TE link signaling, graceful TE link deletion, constrained multi-region signaling, adjustment capacity advertisement, coordination of management information bases, and OAM control.

today: RFC 5339 remains a key architectural reference for multi-layer and multi-region GMPLS networks. It has guided subsequent work on protocol extensions and implementation guidance. The separation of what requires protocol changes from what is operational policy has proven valuable as networks have grown more complex.

sections.title: GMPLS and Multi-Layer Networks
sections.content:
GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) extends traditional MPLS to control different types of switching technologies: packet switching, layer-2 switching, time-division multiplexing (TDM), wavelength switching, and fiber switching. Each switching type defines a region in the network. A Multi-Layer Network (MLN) is a single traffic engineering domain that contains multiple switching layers controlled by one GMPLS control plane. A Multi-Region Network (MRN) is a domain with at least two different switching types, either on the same device or different ones, under unified control.

This RFC evaluates whether the existing GMPLS protocols defined in RFCs 3945, 4202, 3471, and 3473 meet the requirements for MLN and MRN operation as specified in RFC 5212. Where gaps exist, it identifies whether extensions are possible or if the functions lie outside protocol scope.
sections.eli5: GMPLS is the control system for networks that use different switching technologies (like packet and wavelength). This section explains what multi-layer and multi-region networks are, and that the document is checking if existing GMPLS works for them.

sections.title: Key Concepts for Multi-Layer Operation
sections.content:
In multi-layer networks, lower-layer LSPs (Label Switched Paths) form a Virtual Network Topology (VNT) that provides connections for upper-layer traffic. When traffic demands change, the VNT must be reconfigured: FA-LSPs (Forwarding Adjacency LSPs) are created and released. This requires several functional components: discovery of the TE topology, collection of traffic demands from the upper layer, a Virtual Network Topology Manager (VNTM) to decide which FA-LSPs to set up or tear down, path computation (possibly via a Path Computation Element), and signaling to establish the LSPs.

Virtual TE links are a key concept: they represent potential connections advertised before the underlying FA-LSP is fully provisioned. When an upper-layer LSP attempts to use a virtual TE link, triggered signaling immediately provisions the underlying FA-LSP if resources are available. Virtual links provide stability (the upper layer sees a stable topology even if lower-layer LSPs change) and flexibility (path computation can use links without waiting for data plane activation).
sections.eli5: Multi-layer networks change their structure over time as traffic needs change. Lower layers provide connections to upper layers. Virtual TE links let upper layers assume they can use a link even before it is fully set up, and the lower layer builds it when needed.

sections.title: Protocol Gaps and Required Extensions
sections.content:
The evaluation identifies that many MLN/MRN requirements can be met by existing GMPLS or are outside protocol scope entirely. However, six areas require new extensions:

Virtual TE link signaling: Current GMPLS signaling cannot set up and release virtual TE links. Two approaches are proposed. The Soft FA approach sets up the FA-LSP in the control plane without activating data plane cross-connections, allowing admission control but requiring state maintenance at all transit LSRs. The remote association approach exchanges virtual TE link IDs between endpoints without transit state, reducing overhead but limiting admission control.

Graceful TE link deletion: Before deleting an FA-LSP, all upper-layer LSPs using it must be rerouted to avoid disruption. This requires mechanisms similar to those for graceful TE link deletion, possibly using the GR-SHUT procedure where a transit LSR notifies the head-end that a TE link will be torn down and withdraws its bandwidth.

Multi-region signaling constraints: When a node can choose between multiple switching capabilities along a path, existing GMPLS signaling cannot specify which capabilities are allowed or excluded. An extension must allow indicating permitted switching capabilities.

Adjustment capacity advertisement: Hybrid nodes (those with multiple switching capabilities) have internal links with finite capacity for adapting signals between switching types. Current GMPLS routing cannot advertise these adjustment capacities when link bundling is used, creating scalability limitations. Routing extensions must advertise adjustment capacities as a new TE link attribute.

Additionally, management coordination via a new MIB module to link separate layer MIB entries, and OAM control extensions to coordinate technology-specific OAM processes are identified as needed.
sections.eli5: The evaluation finds six things GMPLS needs to add: (1) signaling to set up virtual connections, (2) graceful cleanup when removing lower-layer links, (3) ways to specify which switching types are allowed on a path, (4) advertising how much capacity each hybrid node has to adapt between different types, (5) a management tool to link information from different layers, and (6) ways to control checking and troubleshooting across layers.

sections.title: Functions Outside Protocol Scope
sections.content:
Several critical MLN/MRN requirements are correctly identified as lying outside the scope of GMPLS protocols and belonging to implementation and operations:

Virtual Network Topology Management: Deciding which FA-LSPs to create or tear down, when to do so, and how to optimize the VNT according to traffic demands is a management and operational decision, not a protocol function. The VNTM component that makes these decisions is implementation-specific. Similarly, path computation for the VNT can be distributed across network elements or centralized at a Path Computation Element, independent of VNT management decisions.

FA-LSP attribute inheritance: When an FA TE link is advertised, its parameters inherit from the FA-LSP parameters according to local policies. This is a matter of operational configuration and coordination between head-end and tail-end nodes, not a protocol-level requirement.

Stability: Protecting the upper layer from VNT changes relies on traffic engineering and VNT management algorithms that minimize perturbations by retaining existing paths when computing new VNTs. This is a matter of algorithm design, not protocol extension.

Scalability: The full-mesh approach (where every pair of border nodes has an LSP between them) creates n² RSVP-TE sessions and can be memory- and CPU-intensive, but decisions about topology design and session management are operational, not protocol-level.

Connectivity verification and OAM: Data plane connectivity verification uses technology-specific mechanisms (SDH uses G.707 and G.783; MPLS uses BFD). The GMPLS protocols provide existing tools like test mode and the Link Management Protocol that aid this function, but the core mechanisms are technology-specific and out of protocol scope.
sections.eli5: Many tasks that sound like they need new protocols are actually things operators and engineers decide: how many lower-layer connections to set up, when to set them up, how to copy settings from one layer to another, and how to check if connections are working. GMPLS already has tools that help, but these decisions are not protocol-level problems.

sections.title: Scalability and Management in MLN/MRN
sections.content:
Scalability of multi-layer routing depends on how the network is organized. If a single routing instance advertises multiple layers, the effect is merely an increase in the number of nodes and links, which modern IGPs handle well. If the network is fully integrated (hybrid nodes with all switching types), there is an increase in the number of Interface Switching Capability Descriptors (ISCDs) per TE link, but each interface rarely supports more than two or three switching types, so the impact is modest (about 36 bytes per ISCD in OSPF).

The number of lower-layer LSPs advertised as upper-layer TE links impacts routing protocol scaling. A full mesh of lower-layer LSPs could create n² TE links where n is the number of layer-border LSRs. VNT management must account for this when deciding which LSPs to provision. Virtual TE links can reduce control plane overhead compared to full-mesh approaches.

For management, existing GMPLS MIB modules can model and control GMPLS switches and signaling protocol operation across multiple layers. RFC 4220 provides TE link management and RFC 4803 covers LSR control. However, an additional MIB module could coordinate management of separate layers to construct a single MLN entity, effectively linking entries in existing MIBs together.

Operations and Alarms (OAM) for multi-layer networks are at an early development stage. Each technology layer typically has its own OAM processes (SDH/SONET, Ethernet, MPLS). GMPLS procedures can coordinate these, for example through route recording to verify paths, status flooding of TE links, test mode for sampling end-to-end characteristics, and the Link Management Protocol for fault isolation. GMPLS signaling also provides Notify messages for fault reporting and alarm collection and distribution along LSP paths, but coordination between layers remains an operational matter.
sections.eli5: When you organize a multi-layer network, you need to think about how many connections to set up (full mesh can be expensive) and how to manage and troubleshoot them across layers. GMPLS has existing tools like management databases and notification messages that help, but operators must decide how to use them.

sections.title: Summary and Outlook
sections.content:
RFC 5339 concludes that most MLN/MRN functions rely on mechanisms that are outside GMPLS protocols: local procedures, policies, TE mechanisms, and algorithms. The six identified areas requiring protocol extensions address essential gaps in controlling virtual topology, managing graceful shutdown, handling multi-region path selection, advertising hybrid node adjustment capacities, coordinating management information, and controlling OAM across layers.

The document provides clear guidance for future protocol development efforts. It emphasizes that where requirements are met by existing GMPLS protocols, no extensions are needed. Where functions lie outside the protocol domain, implementation and operational guidelines are more valuable than protocol changes. The careful separation of what belongs in protocols versus what belongs in operations and management is a key contribution of this evaluation.
sections.eli5: This document is a checklist: it says which multi-layer network features GMPLS already handles, which ones need new protocol rules, and which ones are just matters of how you run your network. It gives clear direction for what to build next.
